ABSTRACT 
Stiff-man syndrome is a rare neurologic disorder characterized by 
progressive, fluctuating muscle rigidity with painful muscle contrac- 
tions affecting predominantly the back and proximal extremities. In 
the ED, the diagnosis can be easily overlooked and misdiagnosed as 
acute or chronic low back pain and muscle spasm. This syndrome is 
often associated with diabetes, autoimmune diseases, and cancer. 
This report describes an illustrative case of a 39-year-old woman who 
presented to the ED with a two-year history of right leg spasms and 
low back pain that had become so severe in the preceding two days 
that she was unable to ambulate. Clues to the patient’s proper di- 
agnosis coincide with the diagnostic criteria for stiff-man syndrome: 
the presence of a slowly progressive stiffness of the axial muscles and 
proximal limb muscles, making ambulation difficult; hyperlordosis of 
the lumbar spine; episodic spasms precipitated by jarring or sudden 
movement; a normal intellectual, sensory, and motor examination 
when not in spasm; and a marked amelioration of symptoms with the 
IV administration of diazepam. High-dose oral diazepam is the main- 
tenance drug of choice.

I The stiff-man syndrome is a rare neurologic disease characterized 
by episodes of progressive, rigid stiffness of the axial and limb mus- 
culature with superimposed painful muscle spasms. The syndrome is 
not well known by emergency physicians (EPs). Because of its non- 
specific presentation, it may be overlooked or erroneously diagnosed 
as a psychiatric disorder, drug-seeking behavior, opisthotonic extra- 
pyramidal reaction to drugs, tetanus, or other musculoskeletal back 
and limb pain. The syndrome is frequently associated with diabetes, 
autoimmune diseases, and cancer. Stiff-man syndrome is usually not 
life-threatening but it can cause significant long-term morbidity. The 
exact mechanism of the disorder is not fully understood but it is 
believed to have an autoimmune basis. Treatment has been successful 
with high doses of benzodiazepines. This case report describes a 
patient who presented to the ED with stiff-man syndrome and dis- 
cusses the diagnosis, etiology, immunology, and management of this 
rare disease. 
I CASEREPORT 
History 
A 39-year-old black woman who had back pain was carried into 
the ED by two relatives. She related that she had had severe, inter-

mittent back spasms over the preceding week. Two days earlier, she 
had seen an orthopedist who had treated her with diazepam, 5 mg 
bid, and chlorzoxazone, 500 mg qid. He had referred her to a neu-

rologist the following day, but upon arrival at the neu- 
rologist’s office, the woman driving the patient had been 
unable to get the patient out of the car due to the 
severity of her back spasms. 
The patient reported similar but less intense low 
back pains and severe right leg spasms over the pre- 
ceding year. Review of her medical record showed a 
history of low back pain with spasms and right lower- 
extremity spasms for about three years. Magnetic res- 
onance imaging of the cervical spine three years pre- 
viously had been unremarkable, and MRI of the lum- 
bosacral spine one year earlier had been inconclusive. 
Electromyography (EMG) performed at that time had 
been inconclusive. 
The patient’s review of systems was significant for 
occasional vomiting when she attempted to take med- 
ications. The patient denied any recent travel or history 
of skin lesions or wounds, fever, chills, night sweats, or 
incontinence. Her past medical history was significant 
for a vitamin B12 deficiency and atrophic gastritis for 
which she received monthly B12 injections. There was 
no history of a psychiatric disorder. Her only other 
medications were those prescribed in the three days 
prior, which included the diazepam and chlorzoxazone 
mentioned above and zolpidem tartrate, 10 mg qh. Her 
tetanus immunization was not current. 
Physical Examination 
On physical examination the patient was alert, ori- 
ented, and anxious, with unremarkable vital signs, ex- 
cept tachycardia during spasms. She had intermittent 
spasms of the trunk with arching posture, lasting 2 to 
5 minutes. These episodes of opisthotonos seemed trig- 
gered by external stimuli (e.g., by opening the door, 
speaking, and tactile stimuli, but not by loud noises). 
Between episodes, the patient was alert and comfort- 
able, and her neurologic examination was unremarka- 
ble. Her cranial nerves were intact and symmetrical; 
her reflexes were +2 and equal bilaterally; there were 
normal tone and strength in all extremities, and sen- 
sation was normal for pain and light touch. Her straight 
leg test was negative bilaterally. 
The patient experienced moderate to severe para- 
spinal spasm, with a mild-moderate hyperlordosis dur- 
ing spasms. During the spasms the patient became op- 
isthotonic and so rigid that continued examination was 
impossible. However, she remained alert and cried out 
in pain. Her abdominal musculature was board-like to 
palpation, with normal bowel sounds. Initial laboratory 
data showed a mild anemia and a serum bicarbonate of 
15 mmoVL, presumed secondary to lactic acid from the 
severe muscle contractions. Electrolytes, WBCs, uri- 
nalysis, creatine kinase, and calcium were within nor- 
mal limits. 
Clinical Course 
The patient was given diazepam, 5 mg IV, with con- 
trol of symptoms for approximately 30 minutes. She 
was admitted to the neurology service with the working 
diagnosis of stiff-man syndrome. Needle EMG showed 
increased volitional activity and poor relaxation, par- 
ticularly in the right tibialis anterior and lumbosacral 
paraspinal muscles in association with severe spasm. A 
lumbar puncture for anti-glutamic acid decarboxylase 
(anti-GAD) antibodies was done. (Several months after 
discharge, a positive result was obtained.) A placebo 
saline challenge test showed no relief of spasm. The 
patient was treated with increasing doses of diazepam

and her symptoms were finally controlled on a 10-mg 
qid dose. She was discharged after four days in the 
hospital with the diagnosis of probable stiff-man syn- 
drome.
